cue.heading: Displacement vs. preemption
cue.text:
Federal rules developed by courts for particular subjects of national concern.

Displacement occurs when Congress legislates on a question those rules governed. Whether a statute also preempts state law is a separate inquiry.

evidence.quote: a new federal common law has emerged for subjects of national concern.
Legislative displacement of federal common law does not require the “same sort of evidence of a clear and manifest [congressional] purpose” demanded for preemption of state law.

private_notes: Reader: Haiku 5.5 subagent scanned all 682 blocks and proposed 45 opportunities (scan.json); editor checked each against the transcript and sources, selected 22 (18 recommended). Later edits (2026-10-15) bring the set to 27 cards, 24 recommended.

Omitted as passing or self-explaining: tobacco/opioid analogy (Kagan explains it), Kurns, Missouri v. Illinois / Tennessee Copper, Phillips v. Shutts and BMW v. Gore (name-drops in Harris's opening), equal sovereignty / extraterritoriality / source-state / constructive-presence glossaries (advocates define the terms on the spot), dormant Commerce Clause glossary, the respondent-named-in-state-proceeding comparison.

Omitted as redundant with speech: AEP's expert-agency passage (Kavanaugh reads it verbatim at 102:10), Ouellette's 'implicit corollary' (Kavanaugh quotes it at 75:43), the trial court's causation ruling (Shanmugam reads it at 49:44).
Not done: C.A.R. 4.2 vs. C.A.R. 21 comparison at 23:02 (official Colorado rule text not fetched; the Rule 21 question is disputed, so a card risks taking a side).
Gorsuch (57:34) says EPA disclaimed power over stationary sources too; the Federal Register shows that as a proposal (91 FR 59002, Sept. 17, 2026), so the card labels it 'Proposed rule'.
Transcript block 498 says "RICO's regulation"; the case is Puerto Rico Dept. of Consumer Affairs v. Isla Petroleum, 485 U.S. 495 (1988), about Puerto Rico's gasoline price regulation.
Atlantic Richfield: no vote shown; Oyez records one 7–2 decision, but the jurisdiction holding was unanimous, which the card states.
Default-hidden: Pork Producers (nuanced: it rejected an extraterritoriality rule while Shanmugam cites it for territorial limits) and Commonwealth Edison (Sotomayor already summarizes it).
Justice Alito did not participate (Clerk's letter, Sept. 28, 2026); the argument does not discuss it, so no card.

Merged from the Codex set (2026-10-15): AEP and Ouellette introductions, displacement-vs-preemption glossary, parties’ starting-point comparison, and the shorter wording of the question presented. Official syllabi fetched from govinfo (U.S. Reports 479 and 564).
Ouellette footnote 20 now quoted from the official U.S. Reports PDF (govinfo), replacing the earlier main-text substitute.

Neutrality pass: cards should give background or show what is being discussed, not referee a disputed point. Colorado Rule 21 excerpt hidden for that reason; Commonwealth Edison text trimmed; Codex’s “relief Boulder seeks” card not adopted (outside material corroborating one side’s characterization).
